📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a significant part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he noted.

It has been revealed that “His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between demonstrates across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and Newly introduced Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

In a recent development, “That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time reveals were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

Industry observers note that “We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

It has been revealed that J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent shows at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

#148543. For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

📅 20 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends.
  • Sources indicate that “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF.
  • Sources indicate that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

Sources indicate that “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

Sources indicate that so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she says, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

So for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one big difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she states. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”.

Caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

“It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she says. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”.

The reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

It has been revealed that dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell claims. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”.

Sources indicate that from a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell claims she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”.

The bigger glitch is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she states. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”.

According to recent reports, caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”.

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the company’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but indicates that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

Dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He says that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”.

Recent findings suggest that and then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”.

According to recent reports, whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger complications that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she notes. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”.

Industry observers note that given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, states Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

Since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she says. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”.

It has been revealed that dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she says. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”.

Industry observers note that it’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a proposal in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s crucial to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she notes, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”.

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that following a European tender procedure, the Municipality of Zutphen, Netherlands, has appointed Mecanoo to transform the existing Theatre Hanzehof & Buitensociëteit into a cultural destination. The project, called Hanzehuis, was developed in collaboration with Hanzehof theater, de Muzehof center for the arts, and BIJ de Bieb library, and with ABT Consulting engineers and building services consultant Nelissen. It involves designing a fresh center for culture, knowledge and exchange, preserving the main historic building and introducing a new volume to accommodate cultural activities, education and community life under a single roof. Mecanoo contributed to the preparatory phase, and this appointment marks the transition to developing the design further with the professional team, the Municipality and the participating cultural organizations.

Following a European tender procedure, the Municipality of Zutphen, Netherlands, has appointed Mecanoo to transform the existing Theatre Hanzehof & Buitensociëteit into a cultural destination. The project, called Hanzehuis, was developed in collaboration with Hanzehof theater, de Muzehof center for the arts, and BIJ de Bieb library, and with ABT Consulting engineers and building services consultant Nelissen. It involves designing a newly introduced center for culture, knowledge and exchange, preserving the main historic building and introducing a new volume to accommodate cultural activities, education and community life under a single roof. Mecanoo contributed to the preparatory phase, and this appointment marks the transition to developing the design further with the professional team, the Municipality and the participating cultural organizations.

The Theatre Hanzehof & Buitensociëteit in Zutphen was designed by architect D. Lijsen in 1891. The building was a private social club and concert hall on the edge of the historic Hanseatic city center, noted for its coffered neoclassical ceiling and good acoustics. Since then, it has been renovated and expanded on numerous occasions, including repairs of bomb damage and expansions to modernize the theater. It served as a congress center, theater hall and cinema until 2020, when it was decided to refocus it as a cultural platform. Centrally located within a park-like landscape, the current premises offer the local public a modern theater hall of 550 seats and a concert hall of 600 seats, which host 120 professional concerts and performances per year as well as events by regional groups and social organizations, reaching approximately 75,000 visitors annually.

Industry observers note that mecanoo's Hanzehuis proposal aims to respect the site while introducing a new volume to accommodate both traditional and new programming. Across the preserved main theater hall, the historic Buitensociëteit and a new timber volume, the cultural center will bring together a theater hall, music and dance studios, a café and flexible spaces for study, work, learning and leisure. According to Mecanoo, the ensemble was conceived as "a living room for the city" rather than "a collection of venues." The different program areas are connected by an interior route called De Straat (The Street), which links the historic structures, the new building and the surrounding park. This circulation space is conceived as an area for informal encounters between visitors, performers, students and the wider community, designed to be transparent, open and accessible. The flexible program supports a broad range of activities, from children's theater and pop concerts to workshops, educational programs and spontaneous gatherings. The center is envisioned as a place where Zutphen's heritage and contemporary cultural life come together.

RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.
  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework at the moment only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson stated his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he stated he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

Industry observers note that “I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Industry observers note that williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The company describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” noted Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The organization’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

#148536. It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

📅 21 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2298 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day.
  • Industry observers note that I have just seen Michael (the latest Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release.
  • On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

Industry observers note that I have just seen Michael (the latest Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She notes almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

Sources indicate that “There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she states. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

Long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she indicates. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

“The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

It has been revealed that once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft new stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

Industry observers note that “This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

According to recent reports, in talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

Recent findings suggest that she laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

In a recent development, “The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

That clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

“I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is significant. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

In the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she indicates. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

It has been revealed that long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

Industry observers note that “I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

Industry observers note that “In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she states. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother stated it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a newly introduced idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

In a recent development, but Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

Industry observers note that “I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”.

Beauty was never her primary currency, she notes. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

Industry observers note that “Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she claims. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the major stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

Breaking: Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in latest directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” stated Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that he saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she mentioned. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually established themselves among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an key influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” remarked Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… traveling the world as much as we to can see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

According to recent reports, alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its thought thorugh eclecticism.

According to recent reports, “We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that it’s very key and it’s gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell is size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo stated there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

Industry observers note that “Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto stated if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

It has been revealed that “If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

In a recent development, to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

#148532. Latest Update: How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1476 w)

Latest Update: How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
  • The term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
  • Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

The term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to crucial resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a big role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

In a recent development, the reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

Sources indicate that that can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman states. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Sources indicate that ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

Sources indicate that going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

It has been revealed that again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

According to recent reports, you could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

If you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your intends could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

In a recent development, that said, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, indicates Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

In a recent development, feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, says Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

Still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Goodman notes the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

It has been revealed that yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, indicates Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

All of that is normal, says Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

According to recent reports, you can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact proposal you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, claims Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

In a recent development, remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction tech giant Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley remarked the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently revealed that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) revealed the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

Architecture is commonly examined through its visible form, materials and spatial organisation. The physical fabric of a building can also retain evidence of events and alterations that are not apparent from its present appearance. Cracks, repairs and structural changes may indicate when and how a building was modified, while photographs and material fragments can provide further evidence about the circumstances surrounding those changes. Forensic investigation examines these traces, using the built environment and its surrounding records to establish how particular events, alterations or failures occurred.

Differences in brickwork, inserted structural members or paint layers beneath later finishes can help establish the sequence of these changes. Compared with historical drawings and photographs, such details can indicate when different parts of a building were constructed, replaced or altered.

The investigation of the Beirut Port Explosion on 4 August 2020 illustrates how separate visual records can be assembled into a spatial reconstruction. Working with the Egyptian publication Mada Masr, Forensic Architecture examined photographs and videos recorded from different parts of Beirut to reconstruct the sequence of events at Warehouse 12.

The investigation of the Beirut Port Explosion on 4 August 2020 illustrates how separate visual records can be assembled into a spatial reconstruction. Working with the Egyptian publication Mada Masr, Forensic Architecture examined photographs and videos recorded from different parts of Beirut to reconstruct the sequence of events at Warehouse 12.

Investigators geolocated individual videos and plotted each camera's field of view against a three-dimensional model of Beirut. Footage without metadata was synchronised by comparing changes in the shape and movement of the smoke plumes. The analysis identified four separate plumes emerging from different parts of the warehouse over approximately fourteen minutes. Photographs from January 2020 and a video recorded in December 2019 were also used to reconstruct the warehouse interior. This model helped investigators estimate the area occupied by the 2,750 bags of ammonium nitrate.

It addresses the credibility and authenticity of sources, the context in which material is collected and the safety of those who provide it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

The low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

According to recent reports, dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.
  • After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew.
  • It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

In a recent development, our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

We thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Industry observers note that our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

Not only were Ethan and I fresh to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

If we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

Sources indicate that during our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

According to recent reports, our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

The months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

It has been revealed that so how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

It has been revealed that when we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

Ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

According to recent reports, when we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

Sources indicate that we decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

It has been revealed that fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor newly introduced experiences together.

We found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.

3 Signs You’re the ‘Fringe Friend’ of Your Group, According to a Psychologist

💡 Key Takeaways
