How to Take Your Breathwork to the Next Level

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975.
  • Pranayama—the practice of controlling your breath—is a difficult art to practice, one that requires years of persistence and patience.
  • Recent findings suggest that A thorough familiarity and regular practice of the first three limbs of yoga—yama, niyama, and asana—are essential before beginning a serious pranayama practice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975. This article about pranayama practice tips first appeared in the March-April 1983 matter of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Pranayama—the practice of controlling your breath—is a difficult art to practice, one that requires years of persistence and patience. The student may begin at a simple level with breathwork and breathing exercises, cultivating the intelligence of the breath in a step by step manner; but because the practice of pranayama brings about profound physiological and psychological transformations, it should not be approached casually or carelessly.

Recent findings suggest that A thorough familiarity and regular practice of the first three limbs of yoga—yama, niyama, and asana—are essential before beginning a serious pranayama practice. The moral foundation of the yamas and the self-discipline of the niyamas prepare the student to use wisely the power that pranayama generates. A regular asana practice is important for several reasons. Pranayama is very demanding on the nervous system, and the asanas help to “rewire” the body, enabling it to safely handle the increased voltage (prana). Secondly, the attention to postural detail and the concentration required in asana practice prepare the mind to stay quietly alert to changes in the musculoskeletal system. Pranayama involves continued subtle adjustments in posture to maintain correct alignment and allow complete freedom of the breath. Thirdly, regular asana work develops a strong, flexible spine, an open chest and loose hip joints—indispensable attributes for seated pranayama.

Industry observers note that the serious student of yoga must also intuitively understand the importance of abhyasa and vairagya before beginning pranayama. Patanjali, in the twelfth sutra of the Samadhi Pada, introduces these two most essential means for calming the mind. Abhyasa is constant practice. It will take years of steady, often boring work to advance beyond the beginning stages of pranayama. While contemporary society often expects immediate results from any investment of time or energy, pranayama requires day-to-day diligence without expectations. The mind must slow down. This attitude of dedicated persistence secures a steadiness of the mind that allows the pranayama practice to flourish.

According to recent reports, vairagya is the absence of desire, the surrender of the ego. It allows the universal Self, the atman, to become manifest. This creates a receptive mental state in which the mind is passive yet alert, free of actively created thoughts, fantasies or daydreams. This silent state allows the more subtle stages of pranayama to be observed and experienced. The egoless innocence of vairagya is of crucial importance for another reason. Pranayama magnifies and amplifies the mindset of the practitioner. Greed and desire for enlightenment or spiritual powers while practicing pranayama can entrap the yoga student in a nightmarish world of subconscious creations. All images and ideas that appear on the mental screen are illusions and should be observed and dismissed as such. To cultivate silence of the mind, one must let go of all mental activity and draw consciousness inward.

Pranayama is usually done in the sitting position. Hero Pose (Virasana), the Sage or Seer Pose (Siddhasana), and Bound Angle Pose (Baddha Konasana) are all possible postures. Lotus Pose (Padmasana), however, is the pose of preference because it is the strongest and most stable of the sitting poses. Either Half Lotus or a simple cross-legged pose is also suitable, as tight hip joints may make the Lotus difficult to hold for any length of time. Whatever the position, do not allow the knees to be above the hip joints.

Keep your pelvis perpendicular to the floor, release the spine upward, maintaining the normal spinal curves, and distribute the weight evenly across the two sitting bones. The spine should not collapse or waver. Practice sitting against a wall or an outside corner to learn to sit with an erect spine.

All sitting pranayama requires the use of Jalandhara Bandha, a chinlock that regulates the flow of prana between the heart and the brain. The head hangs down from the base of the neck and the sternum is lifted up (not from the diaphragm!) and pressed toward the chin. Do not press the chin to the chest, or push the lower ribs forward. When doing Jalandhara Bandha in pranayama, be sure not to collapse the spine when the head drops. Maintain the lift of the rib cage. The head will tend to lift during inhalations. Observe this and learn to keep the head down in all stages of the breath.

According to recent reports, the best time to practice is in the early morning when the mind is fresh and outside disturbances are at a minimum. Warm up the body with asanas that open the chest and pelvis. Downward-Facing Dog Pose (Adho Mukha Svanasana), Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvanghasana), passively supported if possible, and Reclining Hero (Supta Virasana) are excellent preparatory poses. Strenuous backbends such as Upward-Facing Bow Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) are too agitating to the mind and should not be done before pranayama. This five-to-ten-minute warm-up is not to be confused with a regular asana workout.

Begin a pranayama practice at a simple level. Five-to-ten minutes a day are enough. Gradually, over a period of one to two years, one may increase to 20-to-25 minutes per session, but there is no hard and fast rule on how long to practice. Use the quality of the breath as a guide. There should never be strain or forcing of the breath. When the breath loses its soft rhythm and becomes harsh and irregular, the practice should end.

According to recent reports, because in the beginning sitting upright is often a challenge to one’s attention, pranayama can be practiced in Savasana (the Corpse Pose). A folded blanket placed length-wise under the spine helps open the rib cage and awaken the spinal intelligence. Here, one may focus totally on the breathing process, and sitting can be practiced separately. Later, as breathing and sitting both become more natural, they may be combined.

In a recent development, until sufficient softness and control are developed, advanced techniques such as alternate nostril breathing and long retentions will strain the diaphragm and the brain. The process of refining the breath should begin with an awareness of normal breathing patterns. Most people breathe unevenly and alternate from one lung to another during each breath. In Savasana, learn to observe your own peculiarities. Become sensitive to the movement of the abdomen, the diaphragm and the rib cage. Train the ears to monitor the sound of the breath. Notice the natural pauses between inhalations and exhalations. From this passive observation, you can see what areas require more attention. See how the conscious mind interferes with the breath. Just as in asana practice, pranayama involves letting go of habits. Learn to release blockages that prevent the spontaneous flow of the breath.

It has been revealed that within a few weeks, as you start to develop a sensitivity to the breath, you may begin active experimentation. See your pranayama practice as an investigation of the breath and its effects on the mind and body. Explore different parts of the torso in isolation. Practice breathing into and filling the pelvis. Be creative in discovering how to awaken the intelligence in all the respiratory muscles. Tune in to the diaphragm and learn to move the sides rather than the center of this important muscle.

Try holding the rib cage open during exhalations by maintaining the grip of the intercostal muscles. This will help increase the elasticity of the diaphragm. Because the control centers of the brain will respond more readily to images than intellectual concepts, visualizations can be useful in exploring and opening the thoracic cavity.

Feel the body growing longer (from the sitting bones to the collar bones) as the breath flows parallel to the spine. Feel the breath moving laterally, widening the body at the pelvis, diaphragm and upper chest. Feel the space between the front and back ribs increasing as the breath deepens the chest cavity. Imagine the breath expanding radially from points in the center of the pelvis, diaphragm and rib cage. Let the inhalations and exhalations flow through the back ribs. This is a difficult but important part of the body to get in touch with. Feel the elasticity of the skin as the body expands and contracts.

You will also want to explore inhalations and exhalations. They can be studied independently in a simple deep breathing exercise. After a normal exhalation, take a slow deep inhalation. Repeat the cycle…normal exhalation and slow, deep inhalation.

Reverse the process and observe the differences. Learning to control the flow of air through the glottal opening in the throat will allow you to slow the breath down smoothly. In Sama Vrtti (same vibration) pranayama, the length and quality of the inhalations and exhalations are equalized in a sine wave pattern, and the two phases flow into each other smoothly.

Recent findings suggest that practice this by adjusting the phase you are most comfortable with (either inhalation or exhalation depending upon the individual) to match the other. Develop a softness and consistency to the breath. Short fluid cycles are better than longer, rougher ones. Active breathing is not aggressive breathing!

Sources indicate that the practice of Viloma pranayama can be added after experience with Sama Vrtti is developed. In this form (meaning literally “against the hair”) the inhalations or exhalations do not proceed continuously, but are broken into several stages. In Savasana, begin with a normal exhalation. Then divide the inhalation into three equal parts with a brief pause between each part. Follow this with a slow, deep exhalation. Repeat the cycle of three part inhalation and slow, deep exhalation and continue for several minutes. Take several normal breaths and then reverse. After a slow, deep inhalation, break the exhalation into three equal parts with short pauses between steps. Repeat this cycle for several minutes. Observe the effects. There should be no strain at any time during the breathing. You may also use four or five steps instead of three in your Viloma practice if that feels more comfortable.

Industry observers note that in all breathing practice, keep the mind passive yet alert. The eyes should be closed, but not tense, and the visual energy drawn inward and downward to the center of the chest. There should be no tightening of the diaphragm. No pressure should be felt in the eyes or ears. Breathe only through the nostrils.

To maintain sufficient softness, do not go beyond your capacity. When the breathing becomes too harsh or difficult, stop. Be bold and cautious at the same time. Always lie in a totally passive Savasana for at least five-to-ten minutes after pranayama to allow the mind and body to relax completely. Theoretically, breathing should be a spontaneous process. What could be easier than inhaling and exhaling?

However, interference of the mind induces tension and resistance. The practice of pranayama will help to liberate the breath, and with this freedom comes improved psychological and physiological well-being. The practice of pranayama increases concentration.

Thus prepared, the yogi is ready for the most subtle and difficult inner quest of dharana (concentration), dhyana (meditation) and samadhi (spiritual absorption)—the last three limbs of the Ashtanga Yoga. With these practices, the last traces of ignorance are burned away, and the individual consciousness and the Universal Self merge in yoga’s ultimate union.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Fall riding season is winding down, but Black Friday is right around the corner. Several e-bike companies and retailers have already rolled out great deals and special promotions on some of our favorite and best-tested electric bikes. Now’s the time to score significant savings on an e-bike if you’re shopping for a holiday gift or for yourself.

There isn’t a single type of electric bike or e-bike rider. These zippy, pedal-assist bikes are perfect for enjoying your local bike paths, riding rail trails with your family, or tackling singletrack adventures. E-bikes are also great for your daily commute, basic transportation, and running errands.

With big savings from brands, now is a great time to score a deal to get some rides in before the snow starts falling!

Sources indicate that no matter your budget or riding needs—from commuters to mountain bikers, experienced cyclists and brand-fresh riders—there is an e-bike for everyone and every age. Our test team rides dozens of electric bikes each year, and these are some of our favorites and the best deals out there right now.

According to recent reports, the Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. The Level platform has proven to be reliable, low-maintenance, and fun to ride—and it doesn’t break the bank.

It has been revealed that the REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. The bike also has regenerative braking, upping the range to 75 miles. For commutes and running errands, the Level comes standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Riders will also find the Level’s connected features very useful. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

Compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s fresh torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that issue. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

Sources indicate that the Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same major, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Recent findings suggest that aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

The Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike tech, but it helps you get out and enjoy some rides without busting your budget.

The Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Fast Charger, Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

These prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, remarked Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

If you want power and range in a small package, the XP4 750 is right for you. It’s a fast, zippy Class 3 e-bike (pedal assist up to 28 mph) with a 330-pound payload capacity. To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

Sources indicate that the XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

In a recent development, however, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

With a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

In a recent development, to power the Adventure, Cannondale uses a Bafang 750W rear hub motor and an easy-access 750 Wh removable battery. With its power and wide-range 8-speed drivetrain, you will get up every hill, while Tektro hydraulic disc brakes will control your speed on descents. Plus, it’s available in flashy red or more subdued matte black.

At $1,200, this Cannondale is 45% off its original price and is equipped with better parts than many lesser-known brands’ bikes priced hundreds more.

Many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

It has been revealed that REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

According to recent reports, salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Sources indicate that electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

Industry observers note that weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

It has been revealed that electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

In a recent development, velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Electric bikes are a great way for older riders to enjoy cycling and stay active. However, many commuter e-bikes have high top tubes, and even many step-through-style frames still require riders to swing their leg over the frame. The Velotric Discover has a Euro-style, low-step-through frame that makes it easier to get on and off.

Additional comfort features include an adjustable-rise stem, wide seat, and suspension seatpost. The Discover has a 28mph top speed and about 75 miles of range. At 63 pounds, it’s not super light, but it weighs less than many similarly priced e-bikes.

Tech Report: Both Men and Women Are Quitting Running Because of Undiagnosed Pelvic Floor Problems. Experts Want to Break the Taboo So More Runners Can Get Help.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.
  • Sources indicate that “What fresh hell is this?” Liz B.
  • Industry observers note that this was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.

Sources indicate that “What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” notes the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.

Industry observers note that this was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.

Industry observers note that liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz states. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”.

Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research highlights that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.

Sources indicate that as much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these challenges. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, notes Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.

It has been revealed that “Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”.

The good news is these complications can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional. But pelvic floor muscles are like any other muscles in your body. “They need training, they need relaxation, they need strengthening, and they need attention,” indicates Sara Reardon, DPT, WCS, a board-certified pelvic floor physical therapist in Newly introduced Orleans. And finally, we need to stop accepting pelvic floor issues as normal. “When we normalize pelvic floor conditions, they don’t get treated,” says Reardon. “Pelvic floor problems are common, but not normal, and it’s the conversations about them that need to be normal.”.

Here’s what you need to know to keep your pelvic floor in shape and your running on track.

According to recent reports, your pelvic floor consists of a group of muscles going from your pubic bone, which is located just below your abdomen, to your tailbone, which is at the bottom of your spine. It holds and protects the bladder, urethra, vagina, prostate, bowel, rectum, and anus. Were you able to “hold it” until you got to the bathroom? That’s your pelvic floor on the job. Couldn’t wait until you reached home and had to go immediately behind a tree or a parked car? Your pelvic floor may have clocked out. Got an erection? That’s in part thanks to your pelvic floor. Had a vaginal birth? Your pelvic floor was working triple overtime. Had a great orgasm? Yup, it chimes in there too.

When you think about pelvic floor complications, urinary incontinence likely comes to mind first. In one small study, approximately 46 percent of elite female endurance runners and cross-country skiers reported leaking urine when sneezing or coughing. But urinary incontinence is just one type of pelvic floor disorder—and it’s actually least likely to make a runner seek medical help. “They’re worried they’ll be told to stop running,” Pagliano notes. More often, what draws runners with pelvic problems into an expert’s office are other symptoms: not being able to urinate or defecate, having sharp or nagging pelvic pain, pelvic organ prolapse, or fecal incontinence.

According to recent reports, despite its importance, the pelvic floor is under-researched. “The truth is we’ve never cared about pelvic health as a society,” says Wiebe. It’s been seen as a primarily women’s issue, and historically women are underrepresented in medical research. And because pelvic floor issues are mainly linked to postpartum health, men tend to be left out of the conversation as well; experts are only beginning to understand the impact it has on men.

An hour after Gordon Garner wrapped up the perfect 20-mile training run, he called his wife to let her know he was driving himself to the emergency room.

In a recent development, over the previous year, the then 38-year-old software development manager had been transforming into a runner. He worked his way up from doing a Couch to 5K to prepping for his first marathon. Everything about this long run had gone according to plan: He ran at his goal pace for the upcoming 26.2 miles he wanted to complete in under four hours; he stopped every six miles to hydrate; and he felt so good, he was tempted to keep running. “Stick to the training plan,” Garner told himself, as he wrapped his last mile and headed back to his Dallas home. Before he hopped in the shower, he felt the need to pee but couldn’t. After he washed up, he tried again, and only a few drops came out. The pain was excruciating.

The ER doctors quickly ruled out kidney stones, which Garner feared were causing the pain. To empty his bladder, they had to catheterize him. “I have a pretty high pain tolerance,” says Garner, who once broke both wrists playing basketball and an elbow falling from a bike. “I was in a world of pain when they put the catheter in.” Unable to determine what was going on, the hospital discharged him.

But Garner still didn’t know what was wrong and whether it would happen again—which it did at mile 12 of the marathon he was training for. Once more, he felt the urge to pee, so he stopped at the public restroom, and nothing would come out. He kept running for six more miles before dropping out.

Sources indicate that ultimately, it would take two misdiagnoses, three prescriptions that didn’t resolve the glitch, and several more practitioner appointments until he finally found an answer from a physical therapist. “I know exactly what’s happening to you,” Garner remembers her telling him. She explained that the muscles of Garner’s pelvic floor were continuously contracting and wouldn’t relax. The correct diagnosis was a dysfunction known as hypertonic pelvic floor.

According to recent reports, for years, the main conversation around pelvic floor problems has focused on strengthening weakness through Kegel exercises. And yet that wasn’t the case for Garner, nor is it for many others. The pelvic floor is a complex system of muscles that needs to not only contract, squeeze, and lift, but also relax and release. “Your pelvic floor can be plenty strong but not meeting the demands that are being placed on it because it’s not behaving the way you need it to,” Wiebe indicates. If your pelvic floor is constantly contracting, it’s clearly strong, but it can’t perform any other function at the same time.

But the relationship is not as simple as a weak pelvic floor causing leakage or a strong one leading to retention. A 2021 meta-analysis published in Cureus Medical Journal concluded that even a strong pelvic floor can lead to urinary incontinence. In fact, some young female runners who have never given birth (a life event usually linked to incontinence) can experience urine leakage. “We also have studies showing pelvic floor activation is similar between incontinent and continent runners, so the status of the pelvic floor muscles can’t be the only cause of leakage,” says Wiebe.

Experts like Wiebe consider how your pelvic floor behaves over time—not in just one moment. “If someone doesn’t leak while doing all their regular daily activities, but then leaks at the very end of a 45-minute run, that pelvic floor is pretty strong, but it may not have the endurance for a long run,” Wiebe says. “And if that person only ran 35 or 40 minutes, they might never experience running-related incontinence. Endurance is different from strength and may better explain leaks for some.”.

There is more to pelvic floors than just tightening and relaxing. “A lot of people think the pelvic floor is like a light switch: It’s either on or off,” Pagliano indicates. “In reality, it’s more of a dimmer switch because it has to…transition from very bright to dim or from high to low very swiftly, like when we’re running.” In your body, that transition looks like your pelvic floor muscles lengthening, shortening, and working more or less to match activity demand with every foot strike.

According to recent reports, and the pelvic floor doesn’t act in isolation. “If I have a patient whose balance is off and they don’t have the ability to navigate impact as well through their ankle, knee, and hip, then there’s more work to manage impact that gets kicked up to the pelvic floor,” states Pagliano. “I often joke that the pelvic floor is like the mom of the body. If other muscles are just like, ‘Oh, I don’t want to do that,’ then the pelvic floor has to step up and do it.”.

Colleen Quigley has spent the past five years crisscrossing the globe trying to relieve a nagging source of pain that often prevented her from performing her best. “I had recurring injuries in my left foot, but a lot of the time pain would also show up in my lower back or my hip,” Quigley says. “At a certain point, I wasn’t able to train at a high level anymore.” The steeplechase specialist, NCAA champion, and current world-record holder in the 4 x 1500m relay saw more than 50 different experts, flying at one point to Germany for injections into her back.

Industry observers note that then one practitioner noticed a particular problem. “He muscle-tested me for things that were going on in my pelvis, then he revealed me an exercise to relieve tension and tested me again,” says the 2016 Olympian. “Suddenly all the problems I tested for in my pelvis disappeared.” The exercise? A tongue stretch to relieve tightness in her jaw. “Jaw tension and pelvic floor tension have a relationship,” Wiebe says. “It’s essentially both ends of the alimentary tract.”.

It was a revelation to Quigley and struck a chord with other runners. Quigley’s Instagram video demonstrating the stretch she now uses as part of her warmup routine to help relax her pelvis has gathered more than 42,000 likes. Although a single change wasn’t the solution to all of Quigley’s injuries, the jaw-pelvis connection helped resolve some symptoms that doctors couldn’t explain.

Quigley’s experience illustrates shortcomings in how diagnoses are sometimes made. Doctors and patients often focus on symptoms instead of looking for the root cause. In one study, researchers in Canada screened women who came to an orthopedic clinic for lower back and pelvic pain for pelvic floor muscle dysfunction. The study found that 95 percent of the women with lumbopelvic pain also had underlying pelvic floor dysfunction that needed to be addressed.

And Quigley’s hip pain was likely related to her pelvic issues as well. “We have deep hip stability muscles that are part of our pelvic floor,” explains Reardon. “When people start experiencing a high hamstring strain or they have a deep hip pain they feel like they just can’t get to, that can be often pelvic-floor-related.” And it doesn’t stop there. Reardon states that pain from pelvic floor dysfunction can show up in various and unexpected ways, including during bowel movements and even intercourse, which is why it’s vital to find an expert with experience treating these issues (see sidebar).

Fortunately, the conversation around pelvic floor problems is evolving. “We’re starting to see patterns that might explain why you and I might have the same symptoms but maybe have different ways that we find resolutions,” notes Pagliano. For runners, it might be a matter of your stride, your form, or even your breathing. “If someone holds their abdomen tight while they are running or are constantly holding their breath during normal everyday activities, we often see pelvic floor muscles that have higher tone or activity and actually don’t relax when they should. Sometimes this leads to leakage with running. Just strengthening the pelvic floor below won’t matter if those muscles are already ‘on’ and have lost the ability to contract and relax.”.

Industry observers note that as for Gordon Garner, after finally finding the right therapist, he scaled back his running for a few weeks while working on stretching and breath-control exercises. In 2023, he ran 40 miles in a 24-hour period to celebrate his 40th birthday. “I was a little worried, just because I was testing these newly introduced boundaries, but with my exercises and my breathing techniques, I had no challenges. I’m very in touch with my pelvic floor muscles now.”.

In a recent development, liz finally found a therapist who helped her establish a strength-training routine in order to coordinate pelvic floor muscles again, pay attention to her body’s signals, and get back to running. Twenty months after giving birth, she raced her ninth marathon, without having to worry about leaking midrun. When your pelvic floor isn’t functioning as it should, “you realize that everything you do—breathing, talking, laughing, moving, carrying things—everything involves the pelvic floor,” Liz states.

Industry observers note that with the right help and a better understanding of your body, pelvic floor problems can be solved. It’s a commitment, but your running will thank you. “Clients will always say, ‘Do I have to do these exercises forever?’” indicates Reardon. “I tell them, ‘Yes, to some extent, if you’re going to keep running.’”.

Lauren Garges, DPT, director of pelvic rehab with St. Luke’s University Health Network in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, shares a simple at-home test that can help determine if you’re suffering from an overactive pelvic floor:.

• Sit on a large stability ball or a rolled-up hand towel. There should be pressure on the perineum, the space between the genitals and anus.

• Using the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or gas, imagine you’re trying to vacuum up a marble. Then, actively try to relax those muscles to see if they go back down, like an elevator.

“If they’re too tight, nothing may happen because your muscles are already as tight as they can get,” she notes. “Or you might be able to squeeze upward but cannot feel the downward [release]. That’s a sign of tension.”.

If you find contracting the muscles challenging, Garges claims, it’s a sign of pelvic floor weakness.

It has been revealed that before you start doing kegels—especially if you have incontinence or other pelvic floor problems—see a pelvic floor therapist to ensure it makes sense to add them to your routine, as they’re not for everyone, states Nora Arnold, DPT, a pelvic health physical therapist with Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. If you get the go-ahead, Arnold offers these cues for correct form:.

• It’s best to get the hang of it lying down and then progressing to adding in practice sitting and standing.

• Squeeze your pelvic floor like you’re holding back from passing gas.

• Contract as if you’re stopping the flow of urine (but don’t do this while you’re actually peeing, as it could result in bladder infection).

• Draw your pubic bone and tailbone toward one another.

• Contract as if you are drawing your sit bones together.

• Pull your pelvic floor up as if lifting your bladder toward your heart.

• You need to both squeeze and lift—people forget that second part. Make sure to fully relax the pelvic floor muscles between reps. Breathe through each contraction and relaxation.

• The number of repetitions is best decided by a PT; however, a good place to start is 3x10 contractions, holding for 10 seconds while breathing.

This deep breathing trains coordination between the pelvic floor and the diaphragm. When your diaphragm engages fully, it encourages your pelvic floor to relax and lengthen, Arnold claims.

• To start, lie on your back. You can also do this in child’s pose, happy baby pose, a deep squat, or reclined sitting.

In a recent development, • Breathe in through your nose for four counts. Let your breath be as slow and full as possible. Your pelvic floor should relax and lengthen passively, just like your belly.

• Exhale through your mouth for six counts.

In a recent development, • For maximum benefit, try to incorporate this into your routine for five to 10 minutes a day. But even just 10 repetitions can make a difference.

Check experience / “As a runner, one of the most valuable things you can do is look for a pelvic floor therapist who knows sports medicine and pelvic health,” says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT. If you’re postpartum, you might also seek out someone who has worked with moms; and if you’re male, you might look for a therapist who has experience with male clients. You can find a list of providers through the American Physical Therapy Association. Read online reviews to see what other patient experiences were like.

Recent findings suggest that consider a virtual visit / While some therapy sessions may need to be done in person, many can be done remotely. If there isn’t a great pelvic floor specialist in your area, try working with a therapist online. “I’ve been doing telehealth since before COVID-19,” states Carrie Pagliano, PT. “If I can get a really good sense of why you’re having symptoms by the questions that I ask, you can get resolution. The key is getting the right ‘why.’ After that, the ‘how’ is easy.” Make sure to offer details about whether you were a bedwetter as a child, your birthing history, or when you experience pelvic floor problems, for example.

Don’t stop until you find the right one / Garner, Quigley, and Liz all had to reach out to multiple practitioners before they found the right person. “You don’t try on one pair of pants, say they didn’t fit, and then never wear pants again,” says Reardon. “You have to keep trying different medical professionals until you find the right one.”.

According to recent reports, as the former health director at Family Circle magazine, Lynya developed content to improve the well-being of its 18 million readers. She’s worked as an editor at Glamour, Essence, Seventeen, Heart & Soul, Parenting and more. She also co-edited ESSENCE’s The Black Woman’s Guide To Healthy Living. She received her B.A. in English from Harvard University, integrative health training at Duke, and plenty of life lessons in her hometown of Fresh York City.

The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

But this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

And we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

About the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

What we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

What we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

About the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

What we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” announced over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

Sources indicate that about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. In fact, he thinks of himself as a land animal and has no interest in swimming, which is why I’m gifting him this book from Triathlete contributor Alison Freeman – just to plant the seed. Isn’t that what holiday gifts are for, anyway? Subtle hints wrapped in shiny paper? I think of my brother-in-law, who always gifts his wife exercise equipment even though she is a couch potato; or my mother, who has given me countless hairstyling tools to tame my wild mane into something she deems more respectable.

It has been revealed that but this book will actually serve its purpose, because Freeman has a real talent for making a big, scary goal like a first triathlon approachable and achievable. Her book is a start-to-finish roadmap that eliminates guesswork and leaves the reader feeling like they can not only do a triathlon, but also have fun along the way.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Jon Dorn is a former editor, longtime triathlete, and lifetime gear geek. He’s qualified for six age-group world championships, and loves to bust his butt training for long-course tri. If I hear about a cutting-edge piece of gear, an unconventional training method, or something that’s just plain weird, I call Jon. That said, he’s not afraid to call a spade a spade and let me know if something is just pricey junk; he’s no fanboy.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): I had heard about red light therapy in the context of the general health/beauty space for a few years, but it wasn’t until I was wandering the expo in Kona at this year’s Ironman World Championship that I encountered a red light therapy device that not only targeted triathletes but is also portable. Sadly, the one I checked out on the Big Island was bonkers expensive and didn’t make sense for a gift, so I shopped around for something similar that wouldn’t break the bank. I landed on the reasonably priced Valo Spark that had decent reviews.

On one hand, I’m not 100% sold on the efficacy of red light therapy — and the science is still out on how it works with sports-related aches and pains — but I know Jon trains super hard (his next race is Boulder 70.3 in June), I know he has his share of aches and pains, I know he loves to travel, and I know he likes trying fresh things. Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

The SP Force AXS is our flagship triathlon bike, with a full carbon fiber frame and bars, built with SRAM Force electronic shifting and Zipp 404 Firecrest Carbon wheels. If you want the best performance along with the best value in triathlon, now’s your chance. Our limited BFCM sale is live now.

Industry observers note that about the contributor: Arguably one of the most accomplished triathletes in Triathlete’s contributor lineup, with hundreds of triathlons and well over a dozen Ironmans under her belt, Jordan knows the sport from every perspective. She’s also one of the industry’s best-known and loved figures, representing professional athletes and helping brands grow their businesses.

Recent findings suggest that few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

What we gifted (and why): Jordan might spend more time in the saddle than any of us editors, and she knows her gear as well as anyone, especially what the pros are presently using. While she’s at the moment on the road to recovery from a meniscus tear, we wanted to send her something custom and pro-level to test whether the 3D investment matches the marketing as she rebuilds her fitness on the bike.

But saddles are tricky to gift. Finding this fully adjustable, 3D-printed option gave us the versatility we were looking for: a fit she could fine-tune herself, without being limited to the stock setup straight out of the box.

—Travis Mundell, social media manager.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Zach Nehr is another one of our key tech/gear editors, especially when it comes to indoor training. Blessed (or cursed) by living in the not-winter-compatible state of Wisconsin, Zach is a die-hard Zwifty and has used probably just about every indoor trainer or virtual training platform that exists (or has existed). As much as Zach rides inside, I trust that if he says something is great, it’s great; if it’s not, it’s probably in the dumpster. Because you don’t ride inside as much as he does with junk.

What we gifted (and why): The Profile Design Zwift Ride Supersonic Aerobar was a medium-quiet release during this year’s Hawaii Ironman World Championship week – mostly because you don’t think much about riding in the pain cave when you’re in a tropical paradise prepping for the biggest race of your season. As incongruous as the setting was for an indoor release, I was excited to see that Profile was taking its triathletes seriously by announcing the first-ever triathlon-specific Zwift-integrated aerobar for indoor training.

According to recent reports, I wanted to gift this to Zach because if you dedicate enough time to training indoors, you should really dedicate your indoor training setup as well, not just make do. Being able to control your avatar from a dedicated set of Zwift Ride–compatible aerobars is the pinnacle of tri gear, as it completes the perfect pain cave: the kind that could prep you for next year’s Ironman World Championship, anyway.

In a recent development, about the contributor: When it comes to explaining sports psychology and neuroscience studies to triathletes, there’s no one better than Daya. As a neuroscientist, certified mental performance consultant, and yogi, Daya helps all types of athletes train their brains through her business, and she can make even the nerdiest psychology studies understandable and applicable for triathletes.

Recent findings suggest that what we gifted (and why): When we heard about the Muse Athena S Headband, a “brain-sensing headband,” we thought of Daya. The headband claims it can do everything from tracking your brainwave activity for better focus to tracking your blood oxygenation in the prefrontal cortex to help you build mental endurance. If anyone can sort through the science behind the Muse, it’s Daya, so we’re excited to hear how effective it seems to be in her own athletic performance.

#148442. I Break the Golden Rule of Running Every Race. You Should, Too

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (815 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

I Break the Golden Rule of Running Every Race. You Should, Too

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • There’s an adage that most runners have heard at some point: “Nothing new on race day.”.
  • Industry observers note that it’s simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s an adage that most runners have heard at some point: “Nothing new on race day.”.

Industry observers note that it’s simple. You’re supposed to treat race day how you would your training runs, keeping things like your fueling, shoe choice, and routine similar. The time for experimenting is during the training block. On race day, there shouldn’t be any surprises that could throw you off.

In my decade of competing, rarely has a race day gone to plan. I’ve lost track of the number of times I’ve been thrown off my routine by a traffic jam or a poor night of sleep. By expecting things to go perfectly, you’re almost setting yourself up for failure.

The key to race day, I’ve found, is to be adaptable.

Industry observers note that in the spring of 2024, I signed up for the Brooklyn Half Marathon. I was going to run it as a workout to prepare for my first marathon later that fall.

Recent findings suggest that the day before the race was a disaster. My girlfriend and I drove into Brooklyn on Friday evening to pick up my bib at the expo. What is normally a 90-minute drive took much longer, and we barely made it to the pick-up before it closed. We were both tired and increasingly hangry, and the only thing nearby were some food trucks. So I cut my losses and stomached some greasy buffalo chicken mac and cheese. A far cry from my normal pre-race pasta dinner.

Surely this would come back to bite me, right?

Recent findings suggest that on race morning, things were equally as stressful. I made it to the start line with minutes to spare and not much time to properly warm up. And of course, the lines for the toilets were too long.

But as soon as the gun went off, I felt great. I was comfortable running at my marathon pace and finished with a lot of confidence for my full later in the year.

In a recent development, the experience reinforced that, despite some hiccups, I would still be able to perform to my expectations. I would never initiative to eat fast food or only get 5 hours of sleep, but I didn’t let it bother me too much. When “fresh” stuff pops up on race day, I take it in stride and move on.

According to recent reports, I also believe that there are some things you should intentionally keep new on race day. The day of a race is special; it’s not supposed to be quotidian. Your adrenaline is higher because the stakes are higher, and channeling that energy can be impactful on your performance.

Sources indicate that during my first marathon, I kept a few things special. I wore my favorite lightweight singlet that I sparingly wore during training to keep it pristine. I chose to race in a pair of Nike Alphaflys that I hardly wore during workouts to preserve the foam. I wore my favorite pair of socks and my favorite half tights and my favorite hat. Before driving to the start, I did a 10 minute walk at 5 a.m. at the recommendation of my coach—something I’d never done before—to get the blood flowing.

The idea of nothing upcoming on race day is, in my opinion, incompatible with the essence of race day.

Sources indicate that just look at my marathon. This was my debut at the distance. Everything about the experience was new! The longest I had run was 18 miles, so I was venturing into uncharted territory.

Sources indicate that thankfully, the race went well. I used a massive negative split to hit my goal of sub 2:28, finishing in 2:27:05 for 29th place.

Sure, it’s important to keep some things similar to training. I kept my race fueling proposal the same as my practice runs, and I was diligent about hitting my prescribed pace. But newness is the most exciting part of race day.

Race day is special and you should treat it as such. I hope the novelty never wears off.

In a recent development, theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. In a recent development, diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

Recent findings suggest that our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

Xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

The Chief Customer Officer is a fresh role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay. This is a customer-focused role in the most commercial sense: what a member earns from us, not the feature we shipped, is the centre of every decision.

The measure of success is a Customer P&L that grows on what members hold and keep: LTV:CAC improving, approved-to-paid rising, churn falling, and customer contribution the business can plan against.

This is a banking role, not a requirements-gathering role, a marketing role, or a role you can run from a dashboard. Products are priced on the balance sheet and judged on the money they attract and keep.

This part matters as much as the mandate. The known failure mode for this role, in any organization, is a CCO with a polished customer-insight deck and no ownership of the number. That is disqualifying here.

Day 30: The Customer P&L baseline is documented across retail and institutional: customer contribution, LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, net paid-member growth, and assets attracted and kept. You have formed your own independent view of where members are won, lost, and under-served, and shared it with the CEO and Board.Day 60: The unified Customer operating model is live: one set of key results across Growth, Client Coverage, Mission PMs, and Product Design, read weekly from one source. Every mission PM owns a product's contribution and its price, and the roadmap is ranked on what it earns, built with Finance and the line leads.Day 90: At least one measurable improvement in LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, or net newly introduced AUM flow is live and attributable to a change you made, not a feature ship, an outcome moved. Every cell in your line has defined key results and an owner who explains the number every week.

Impact Globally, Work Remotely.

Shape the FutureImprove lives through cutting-edge technology, work 100% remotely from anywhere in the world.

Great work-life balanceBuild amazing things with a balance of autonomy and collaborative teamwork. Set your own work schedule and make use of a flexible PTO initiative when you need to recharge.

Sources indicate that expect ExcellenceCollaborate, learn, and grow with a high-performance team. Learn how you learn best - from books to conferences, you’ll get a yearly budget for your individual learning and development goals.

At Xapo, we prioritize consumer protection and adhere to regulatory requirements by ensuring that all Xapiens are accountable for upholding principles of fair treatment, transparency, and ethical conduct in their interactions with customers and stakeholders.
